Here is the verse-by-verse commentary on 1 Chronicles 18, drawing on the sources I was able to reach.

---

## 1 Chronicles 18 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

This chapter closely parallels 2 Samuel 8 and forms part of the Chronicler’s selective portrait of David. Chapters 18–20 record David’s wars of conquest that secured the “rest” enabling Solomon to build the temple (1 Chron 22:8–10). Ellicott notes the Chronicler’s habit of abridging, explaining difficult expressions, and adding small details from other sources. The chapter falls into two sections: David’s wars of conquest (vv. 1–13) and his internal administration (vv. 14–17). \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

Martin Selman (Tyndale OT Commentary) observes that the material is “clearly selective, with few details and little analysis of the causes and progress of individual conflicts.” The theological refrain is “the LORD preserved/made David victorious wherever he went” (vv. 6, 13). \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

Matthew Henry opens by noting that the previous chapter recorded David’s piety and prayer; this chapter follows with his prosperity — “for those that seek first the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof … shall have other things added.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

### v. 1 — David Subdues the Philistines
*“Some time later, David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Gath and its villages from the hand of the Philistines.”*

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The Philistines had troubled Israel for centuries. David did not avoid fighting them despite Israel’s long record of losses. He “attacked and subdued these troublesome enemies.” Where Saul’s reign saw Philistines taking territory from Israel, under David “God’s people began to take territory from the enemy.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Precept Austin / Konkel:** David’s earlier wars with the Philistines in 1 Chronicles 14 were defensive. Now they are offensive — “to subjugate enemies, as Nathan the prophet had promised (17:10), to eliminate threat and fear, to provide security and rest.” \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Chronicler gives the plain statement “took Gath and her towns” where 2 Samuel 8:1 has “took Metheg-ammah” (literally “the bridle of the mother-city”), a phrase of uncertain meaning. Possibly it designates a strong position commanding Gath, or describes Gath as the metropolis. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Henry:** Matthew Henry sees a typological foreshadowing: “Thus shall all opposing rule, principality, and power, be, at the end of time, put down by the Son of David.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

### v. 2 — Moab Subdued
*“David also defeated the Moabites, and they became subject to David and brought him tribute.”*

- **Guzik notes a puzzle:** David’s harsh treatment of Moab seems surprising since his great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite and he once entrusted his parents to Moabite care (1 Sam 22:3–4). Guzik suggests “it may be that the Moabites killed or mistreated David’s parents.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Pulpit Commentary** points out that 2 Samuel 8:2 includes the detail omitted by Chronicles: David “measured them with a line… two lines to put to death and one full line to keep alive” — putting two-thirds to death and sparing one-third. The reason for this severity is not stated. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Hill (NIV Application Commentary, cited at Precept Austin):** David apparently leaves local leadership in place but imposes annual tribute as a satellite state of Israel. \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Guzik on “tribute”:** God did not want Israel to destroy every neighbour nation; generally He wanted Israel so blessed that other nations were “taxed” by Israel in recognition of their strength and dominance. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

---

### v. 3 — Defeat of Hadadezer of Zobah
*“As far as Hamath, David also defeated King Hadadezer of Zobah, who had marched out to establish his dominion along the Euphrates River.”*

- **Guzik:** The king of Zobah (a Syrian kingdom) “ran into David on his way to capture territory to the Euphrates.” David’s dominance extended all the way to the Euphrates River. Meyer (cited by Guzik) notes: “The border of Israel was carried to the line of the Euphrates, so that promise made by God to Abraham was fulfilled.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **NET Bible note (cited at Precept Austin):** The Hebrew “to set up his hand” (yad) is usually understood as “control” or “dominion,” but yad can also refer to a monument. Hence the NRSV reads “as he went to set up a monument at the river Euphrates” and the NAB similarly “to set up his victory stele at the river Euphrates.” \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Konkel (cited at Precept Austin):** Kings would set up monuments outside their own territory to represent presence in territory they controlled. It is uncertain whether David or Hadadezer was setting up the monument; the Chronicler’s inference from 2 Samuel 8:3 is that David was doing so. \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Hill:** David opposes Hadadezer’s declaration of sovereignty perhaps because he “has designs on controlling the trade route known as the King’s Highway,” which would explain David’s expansionist policy in the Transjordan. \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Henry:** “Such is the uncertainty of this world that frequently men lose their wealth and power when they think to confirm it. Hadarezer was smitten as he went to establish his dominion.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

### v. 4 — Chariots, Horsemen, and Hamstrung Horses
*“David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and he hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots.”*

- **Textual issue (700 vs. 7,000):** 2 Samuel 8:4 reads “seven hundred horsemen,” not seven thousand. Guzik calls this “probably a copyist error in one of them.” The Pulpit Commentary notes the same and suggests the Samuel reading is to be preferred. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\] \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Deuteronomy 17:16 connection (multiple sources):** Guzik writes that David kept only 100 horses, “showing remarkable self-control and trust in God. David obeyed the principle of Deuteronomy 17:15–16 and absolutely refused to trust in horses as military weapons.” Precept Austin quotes Ron Daniel: “God wanted the king of Israel to be dependent upon the Lord, not on his own military might.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\] \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Precept Austin / Walton (IVP Background Commentary):** Hamstringing was not mere cruelty. Horses could not be “mercifully shot as they are today, and the Israelites had no use for them and no means to care for them; they certainly did not want their enemies to have continued use of them.” Hamstringing involves cutting the rear tarsal tendon (equivalent to the human Achilles tendon). \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Pulpit Commentary** clarifies the translation: it is “more natural to render, David houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved a hundred … he houghed all but a hundred.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Konkel (Precept Austin):** This practice follows the analogy of Joshua 11:6–9, where God requires horses to be disabled and chariots burned. It may be regarded as a stipulation of “holy war” — “all booty of those battles won by direct divine intervention belonged to God and could not be used as plunder.” \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

---

### vv. 5–6 — The Arameans of Damascus Defeated
*“When the Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand men. Then he placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.”*

- **Guzik:** David took what was meant to reinforce the enemy and defeated them too. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Henry:** “The enemies of God’s church are often made to ruin themselves by helping one another. … When hand thus joins in hand they shall not only not go unpunished, but thereby they shall be gathered as the sheaves into the floor (Micah 4:11–12).” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **The refrain “the LORD made David victorious wherever he went”** is identified by all commentators as the theological centre of the chapter. Precept Austin calls it “the key to his success,” reflecting the promise of 1 Chron 17:8–10. The Pulpit Commentary’s homilist (J.R. Thomson) notes the contrast with pagan gods who are destroyers: “Jehovah, it is recorded, ‘preserved David whithersoever he went.’” \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\] \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** In a devotional on this passage, Ligonier connects this refrain to the Davidic covenant: “God had promised victory to His people, and they could trust Him to provide it.” The victory is a gift of sovereign grace, and the proper response is justice and equity in rule. \[https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/justice-and-equity-of-david\]

---

### vv. 7–8 — Gold Shields and Bronze for the Temple
*“And David took the gold shields that belonged to the officers of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Tibhath and Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze, with which Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles.”*

- **Guzik:** The gold shields represent taking “what was the glory of the enemy and transformed it into trophies of the power and goodness of God.” The bronze specifically connects to temple construction — this is why the Chronicler selected these details from 2 Samuel. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Morgan (cited by Guzik):** Even when God shuts the door for us to do a work, we may still be vitally involved: “To be willing to do the work of preparation, when not permitted to undertake the principal service, is proof of real devotion.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Selman (cited by Guzik):** The Chronicler deliberately chose these conquest narratives to show how David was “amassing treasure” for the temple he could not himself build. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Tibhath and Chun replace “Betah and Berothai” in 2 Samuel 8:8 — possibly orthographic variants. The bronze was used for the bronze Sea (laver), the pillars Jachin and Boaz, and various temple vessels. These are detailed in 1 Kings 7 and 2 Chronicles 4. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Henry:** “As the tabernacle was built of the spoils of the Egyptians, so the temple of the spoils of other Gentile nations — a happy presage of the interest the Gentiles should have in the gospel church.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

### vv. 9–10 — Tou (Toi) of Hamath Sends Gifts
*“When King Tou of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer king of Zobah, he sent his son Hadoram to greet King David and bless him…”*

- **Guzik:** Neighbouring nations “saw the hand of God on David and brought him honor and gifts. They knew that a strong, godly leader of Israel was good for the whole community of nations.” David did not treat every pagan nation as hostile; some were friendly. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Selman (cited by Guzik):** The name Hadoram (rather than “Joram” in 2 Sam 8:10) is preferred “since the latter’s Yahwistic form is unlikely in a non-Israelite state.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Henry:** “It is our interest to make those our friends who have the presence of God with them. … It is in vain to contend with the Son of David. Kiss the Son, therefore, lest he be angry.” He applies this typologically to Christ. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Tou had been at war with Hadadezer and had “generally fared the worst in their encounters.” Josephus suggests Tou had been brought into subjection by Hadadezer and now sought to ingratiate himself with David. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

### v. 11 — David Dedicates All to the LORD
*“and King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had carried off from all these nations—from Edom and Moab, and from the Ammonites, Philistines, and Amalekites.”*

- **Guzik:** “When David received this acclaim from the nations he dedicated it all to the LORD. He knew that the praise and glory belonged to God, not himself. David could handle success as well as apparent failure.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Precept Austin / NET Note:** The verb “dedicated” is *qadash* (LXX: *hagiazo*), meaning to set apart or consecrate. David declared the tribute as consecrated to God, separated from all profane use. As one writer noted: “Rather than assume the victor’s right of property, David acknowledged the Source of the victory.” \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

- **Henry:** “That is most truly and most comfortably our own which we have consecrated unto the Lord, and which we use for his glory. Let our merchandise and our hire be holiness to the Lord (Isaiah 23:18).” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The reading “from Edom” is probably correct, whereas 2 Samuel 8:12 reads “from Aram” — unless both places were named in the original source. The mention of Ammon and Amalek may refer to events narrated in the following chapter and in 1 Samuel 30. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Ligonier:** Much of this tribute, including what was taken from conquered and occupied territories, “ended up being used in the temple that Solomon built.” \[https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/justice-and-equity-of-david\]

---

### vv. 12–13 — Edom Defeated; Abishai’s Role
*“Moreover, Abishai son of Zeruiah struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. He placed garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.”*

- **Key difference from 2 Samuel 8:13:** 2 Samuel credits David directly with the victory; Chronicles credits Abishai. The Pulpit Commentary notes the parallel place “omits to say that it was by aid of Abishai.” Psalms 60 (title) probably speaks of an instalment of this campaign. Joab is also credited in 1 Kings 11:15–16. The picture is of teamwork under David’s leadership. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **The Valley of Salt:** Situated in Edom (see also 2 Kings 14:7; 2 Chron 25:11). The Hebrew word used is *gê’* (ravine), not the more generic *‘emeq*. The Pulpit Commentary discusses the uncertain location, noting the traditional identification with the area south of the Dead Sea. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Refrain repeated:** “The LORD made David victorious wherever he went.” Precept Austin calls this the summary of the whole chapter: “Every victory and every enemy subdued was a testimony to the Lord’s preserving power.” \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

---

### v. 14 — David’s Just Reign
*“Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people.”*

- **Guzik:** This shows David was a great king to his own people, not only against neighbouring nations. “He fulfilled what is the fundamental duty of government — to administer judgment and justice (Romans 13:1–7).” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** “David ‘administered justice and equity to all his people,’ the Lord having given ‘victory to David wherever he went’ (vv. 13–14). This was an important encouragement to later Israelites. … Today, this is to be modeled in the church, where leaders are to make decisions according to the justice and equity of God’s law.” \[https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/justice-and-equity-of-david\]

- **Ellicott:** “Executed — was doing; a permanent state of things.” The Hebrew conveys ongoing, habitual action, not a one-time act. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Henry:** “God gives men power, not that they may look great with it, but that they may do good with it. … He was not so intent on his conquests abroad as to neglect the administration of justice at home. Herein … he was an eminent type of the Messiah, the sceptre of whose kingdom is a right sceptre.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

### vv. 15–17 — David’s Officers
*“Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Shavsha was the scribe; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were chief officials at the king’s side.”*

- **Guzik:** “No great ruler succeeds by himself. … Part of David’s success as a ruler was in his ability to assemble, train, empower, and maintain such a team.” We never find such a list for Saul’s government. “There is a limit to what we can be and what we can do for the LORD without order and organization. … order and organization are progress in the Christian life.” \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]

- **Joab** — over the army (military security).

- **Jehoshaphat** — the recorder (*mazkir*). The Pulpit Commentary explains this officer’s “dignity and responsibility and trust … altogether in excess of his duty as mere historical secretary,” involving high-level state record-keeping and counsel. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Zadok and Ahimelech** — priests. Guzik explains there were two priestly centres: one at Gibeon (with the Mosaic tabernacle and altar) and one at Jerusalem (with David’s tent for the ark). Hence two priests. The Pulpit Commentary notes that 2 Samuel 8:17 reads “Ahimelech the son of Abiathar,” but comparison with 1 Samuel 22:20 and 2 Samuel 20:25 suggests the correct reading should be “Abiathar the son of Ahimelech” — a known textual difficulty, with Mark 2:26 supporting the reversed order. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\] \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Shavsha** — the scribe (secretary). The parallel in 2 Samuel 8:17 reads Seraiah, 2 Samuel 20:25 reads Sheva, and 1 Kings 4:3 reads Shisha. The Pulpit Commentary says the differences “are probably due simply to errors of transcription.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **Benaiah over the Cherethites and Pelethites** — Guzik (citing Baldwin on 2 Samuel) says these were “hired soldiers from Crete. By employing foreign guards … David would minimize the possibility of becoming the victim of inter-tribal rivalries.” The Pulpit Commentary notes Geseuius’s view that the names could be translated functionally as “public executioners and public couriers,” though most treat them as ethnic designations. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\] \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

- **“David’s sons were chief officials”** — **A significant textual difference between Chronicles and Samuel:** 2 Samuel 8:18 reads “David’s sons were priests (*kohanim*).” The Hebrew word *kohanim* can mean “priests” strictly, or more generally “princes/chief officials.” The Pulpit Commentary states: “This is, without doubt, the meaning of our text.” The Chronicler (or his source) uses *harishonim* (“chief officials”) to avoid the implication that David’s sons served as cultic priests — something not permitted for non-Levites. Most conservative commentators view Chronicles as clarifying the ambiguous term in Samuel. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

## Traditions Compared

**On vv. 6, 13 (“The LORD made David victorious wherever he went”):**
- **Reformed/Presbyterian (Ligonier):** Emphasises God’s sovereign fulfilment of the Davidic covenant promises. The victory is entirely God’s doing, and the human response is gratitude expressed in justice and equity. \[https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/justice-and-equity-of-david\]
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Emphasises the spiritual-warfare application: David’s victories model how believers fight the world, the flesh, and the devil through trust in God. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]
- **Classic Evangelical (Henry):** “Those who take God along with them whithersoever they go may expect to prosper, and be preserved, whithersoever they go. Those are always under the eye of God that have God always in their eye.” \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-chronicles-18.html\]

**On v. 4 (hamstringing horses):**
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Focuses on David’s faith — refusing to trust in horses, obeying Deuteronomy 17:16, trusting God instead. \[https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-18/\]
- **Konkel (evangelical scholar, cited at Precept Austin):** Sees it as an act of “holy war” — all booty from divinely-won battles belonged to God and could not be used as plunder, following the pattern of Joshua 11:6–9. \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]

**On v. 17 (“David’s sons were chief officials” vs. “priests” in 2 Sam 8:18):**
- Conservative commentators (Pulpit, Guzik) view Chronicles as clarifying that David’s sons were civil administrators, not cultic priests — consistent with the Chronicler’s concern for proper Levitical order. The Pulpit Commentary explicitly states the Samuel term *kohanim* here means “princes,” not priests. \[https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-18.html\]

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes):**
- On v. 3, the NET note suggests that *yad* (“hand”) may refer to a “monument” or “victory stele” rather than “dominion.” The NRSV and NAB adopt this reading: “as he went to set up his monument at the river Euphrates.” \[https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-18-commentary\]
